Swinging flashlight test: for relative afferent pupillary defect
- Light signal from one eye goes to both sides of brain → should stimulate bilateral pupillary constriction response
- Abnormal: both pupils dilate when the light swings to the affected eye → lesion of that optic nerve, in front of the chiasm (e.g. optic neuritis)

EYE MOVEMENTS
Superior rectus: Look laterally and upward
Inferior rectus: Look laterally and downward
Superior oblique: Look medially and downward
Inferior oblique: Look medially and upward
Lateral rectus: Look laterally
Medial rectus: Look medially

Ptosis
- Usually palsy of CN III because it innervates levator palpebrae superioris
Diplopia
- Never a cortical problem → always suspect brainstem and lower: CN III/IV/VI, muscle, neuromuscular junction (NMJ)
Cavernous sinus: contains eye movement nerves (CN III/IV/VI), V1/V2, internal carotid artery
- Also communicates with plexuses (i.e. pterygoid) so can spread eye/facial infection to brain

Pons
- Sensory root forms trigeminal ganglion
- Motor root bypasses ganglion and becomes part of V3

V1 (ophthalmic nerve) - superior orbital fissure
- Branch: frontal nerve exit supraorbital foramen
V2 (maxillary nerve) - foramen rotundum
- Branch: infraorbital nerve exit infraorbital foramen
V3 (mandibular nerve) - foramen ovale
- Branch: mental nerve exit mental foramen
- Branch: auriculotemporal nerve run with superficial temporal artery/vein, anterior to ear going up to temples

V1 (ophthalmic nerve)
- Sensory: upper face, orbit/eye (including scalp/eyelids/nose), cornea
V2 (maxillary nerve)
- Sensory: mid face, upper jaw (including palate)
V3 (mandibular nerve)
- Sensory: lower face/face (including temporomandibular joint (TMJ)), touch/temperature of anterior 2/3 of tongue
- Motor: muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis)

V1/2/3 - touch in 3 sensory locations
V1 - corneal reflex (afferent)
V3 - mastication

Upper motor neuron (UMN) causes of pathology
- Cortical, subcortical, thalamus, brainstem pathology (e.g. stroke/multiple sclerosis (MS))
Lower motor neuron (LMN) causes of pathology
- Compression/inflammation around nerve (e.g. in cavernous sinus)
- Trigeminal neuralgia (from blood vessel pulsating adjacent to nerve)
Medial brainstem between pons and medulla → runs over pons → cavernous sinus

In general (not just for this CN): dysfunction of multiple CNs → brainstem lesion
- e.g. tract of facial nerve wraps around abducens nerve so pontine lesion in that area causes facial weakness and ocular movement issues
Lateral brainstem between pons and medulla, runs with CN VIII
Internal acoustic meatus → stylomastoid foramen → parotid gland (compressed by encapsulating fascia if parotitis, causing facial paralysis)

Motor: muscles of facial expression → 5 branches (The Zoo Buys MANy Cats)
- Temporal: frontalis (sole innervation), orbicularis oculi
- Zygomatic: zygomaticus major, orbicularis oculi, muscles that lift up lip
- Buccal: buccinator, orbicularis oris, zygomaticus major, muscles lateral to oral cavity
- Mandibular: orbicularis oris, mental/chin muscles
- Cervical: platysma (sole innervation)
Special sensory: taste to anterior 2/3 of tongue
Parasympathetic: lacrimal/nasal/palatine/salivary glands

UMN facial weakness: affects contralateral lower face but spares entire forehead
- Due to bilateral cortical innervation of forehead
- Entire forehead can still wrinkle
- Able to close ipsilateral eye weakly (although may not be able to bury lashes)
- Lesions above facial nerve nuclei: cortical/subcortical, corona radiata, internal capsule, descending corticobulbar fibers, brainstem
LMN facial weakness: affects entire ipsilateral face
- Ipsilateral forehead cannot wrinkle, stays smooth
- Ipsilateral eye open wide, cannot close eyelid (vs. an oculomotor nerve (CN III) lesion, which causes ptosis)
- Bell's palsy, parotid gland tumour
- Lesion at or below facial nerve nuclei: nuclei in pons, cranial cavity, middle ear, peripheral nerve distribution
Lateral brainstem between pons and medulla, runs with CN VII
*Internal acoustic meatus → does NOT exit cranium

boxes: Red flags in back and neck painNeurologic, inflammatory, neoplastic, infectious, fracture and vascular red flags suggest a sinister cause; e.g. saddle anaesthesia, night pain, weight loss, fever, IV drug use, osteoporosis.
Mechanical back painAxial pain worse with movement and relieved by rest, midline or peri-midline, with no red flags; often degenerative and 'tweaked' by an acute event.
Who to imageNo red flags and symptoms under 6 weeks: no imaging. X-ray only for red flags or persistent pain despite treatment; CT only if MRI cannot be done.

Discogenic painInternal disc disruption may cause 20-40% of back pain: axial-predominant, mechanical, worse with forward flexion. Managed conservatively with therapy, exercise, NSAIDs or acetaminophen.

Disc herniationCauses both discogenic pain and nerve compression; acute herniation in younger people after lifting, worse with coughing or sneezing; lumbar discs herniate posterolaterally toward nerve roots.

Facetogenic painFacet joint arthritis: localized axial pain, headache in cervical spine, rarely past the knee in lumbar spine; worse with extension, relieved by flexion. Flexion-based therapy, NSAIDs, injections.

Spondylosis and stenosisDegenerative disc disease plus facet arthropathy; progression to subluxation, osteophytes, ligament hypertrophy and spondylolisthesis can narrow neural foramina (lateral stenosis) or the central canal.

Muscle problemsAcute strain/spasm, repetitive strain and myofascial trigger points have no diagnostic test; manage conservatively with reassurance, relative rest, ice/heat, short NSAIDs and physiotherapy.

Whiplash associated disorderAcceleration/deceleration neck injury, most often muscle strain; most improve conservatively: keep moving, avoid C-collars, modest physiotherapy. X-ray if fracture concern, MRI if neurological signs.

boxes: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint problemsAcute injury causes AC separation (grades I-V, increasing displacement); gradual onset suggests osteoarthritis. Grades I-III: education, sling, ice, early exercise; IV-V: surgery.

Shoulder arthritisNoninflammatory: reduced active and passive motion, cuff strength intact, asymmetric joint space, osteophytes. Inflammatory: passive > active motion, weak cuff, symmetric joint space, erosions, osteopenia.
Shoulder replacementAnatomic or reverse arthroplasty: 85% good or excellent, 90% survive 10 years; complications include infection, loosening, instability, fracture.

Shoulder instabilityTraumatic: unidirectional, mostly anterior, 'torn loose', surgery (labral repair) often for young recurrent dislocators. Atraumatic (AMBRI): multidirectional, 'born loose', physiotherapy first, inferior capsular shift.
Glenoid labrumIncreases surface area and depth of the glenoid and acts as a bumper; ligaments, labrum, bones, rotator cuff/muscle forces and nerves all contribute to stability.
Adhesive capsulitisSpontaneous global loss of active AND passive motion with normal X-rays; 2% of adults, 20% of diabetics, onset 40s-50s; freezing, frozen, thawing stages; usually self-limited.

Rotator cuff diseaseMost common shoulder disorder, onset 40s, progressive; intrinsic (vascularity, tendon degeneration) or extrinsic (acromion morphology). Painful arc, Neer and Hawkins impingement signs; staged I-III to arthropathy.
Rotator cuff treatmentMostly nonsurgical: education, NSAIDs, physiotherapy, injections. Stage I: physio or subacromial decompression; Stage II: consider repair; Stage III (full thickness): repair.
Winged scapulaLong thoracic nerve lesion: serratus anterior cannot hold the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall when pushing with the upper limb.
Brachial plexus roots and branchesVentral rami C5-T1: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, terminal branches. Axillary C5-6, musculocutaneous C5-7, radial and median C5-T1, ulnar C8-T1.

boxes: Arm compartmentsAnterior compartment flexes shoulder and elbow and supinates (musculocutaneous nerve); posterior compartment extends shoulder and elbow (radial nerve).

Proximal biceps tendinopathyCommon anterior shoulder pain; tender in intertubercular groove, worse with flexion when supinated. Differential: rotator cuff, bursitis, SLAP tear, arthritis, radiculopathy. Ultrasound helps; physiotherapy is mainstay.
C8 radiculopathy is not shoulder painHigher cervical radiculopathy (C4 or C5) may cause shoulder complaints, but C8 radiculopathy typically gives pain or paraesthesiae in the hand.
Radial nerve in the spiral grooveThe radial nerve (C5-T1) runs in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus, a site at risk of injury; it supplies the posterior compartment.
Brachial artery and humeral fracturesThe brachial artery is used to measure blood pressure and is susceptible to humeral shaft fractures.
Bicipital reflexThe bicipital myotatic reflex tests the integrity of C5 and C6.

Distal biceps ruptureRare but consequential: anterior elbow pain, poor supination and weak flexion after a pop; refer to orthopedics urgently. Proximal ruptures are commoner and usually managed non-operatively.

boxes: Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow)Common (1-3%/year), 30s-40s, mostly occupational. Mainly extensor carpi radialis brevis tendinopathy. Pain just distal to lateral epicondyle, worse gripping and supinating, with resisted middle-finger/wrist extension, and passive stretch.
Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow)Tendinopathy at the common flexor origin. Pain at the origin, with resisted wrist flexion and pronation, and with passive stretch.

Tendinitis vs tendinosisTendinitis is true inflammation (rheumatologic, acute overload, infection); treat inflammation, faster recovery. Tendinosis is collagen degeneration from chronic overuse; more common, slow (100+ days) recovery.

Managing tendinopathyEducate, modify the offending activity, ice/RICE, counterforce strap for tennis elbow, PT eccentric strengthening twice daily for 12 weeks; topical anti-inflammatories; surgical referral if refractory.

Elbow osteoarthritisGradual achy pain, stiffness, loss of range of motion, locking. X-ray: joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts. PT/OT, topical anti-inflammatories, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, steroid injection; arthroplasty if end stage.

Elbow dislocationUsually fall onto outstretched hand (FOOSH); posterior is most common. Red flag: capsule and ligament rupture, ulnar nerve at risk, compartment syndrome. Closed reduction and splint at 90 degrees, or open reduction internal fixation.

Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)Children under 5, girls and left arm more often. Pain after traction on the arm; holds arm flexed and refuses to use it. Closed reduction by pronation and extension; image only to exclude fracture.

Ulnar collateral ligament injuryRepetitive overuse (baseball pitchers); may pop at medial elbow. Medial tenderness, no end point on valgus stress. PT, orthoses; reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) only if needed for function.

Olecranon bursitisMost common superficial bursitis, from a fall on the elbow or repeated leaning. Red, hot, systemically unwell suggests septic bursitis: aspirate and give antibiotics. Otherwise pad, ice, NSAIDs.

Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel)From a hit to the funny bone, leaning, or sleeping flexed. Medial elbow pain, numbness into ring and small fingers, positive Tinel sign; small hand muscles weaken first. EMG/NCS; avoid pressure and hyperflexion.
Pronator syndromeMedian nerve entrapment where it passes between the two heads of pronator teres.

Cubital fossaBounded by brachioradialis, pronator teres and the epicondyle line; holds biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve (TAN), with median cubital vein superficially. Pictured uses: IV access, blood pressure, venipuncture.

Elbow pain by locationAnterior: arthritis, distal biceps. Medial: medial epicondylosis, ulnar neuritis, UCL tear. Lateral: lateral epicondylosis. Posterior: olecranon bursitis, arthritis, triceps tendinopathy. Fracture anywhere.

boxes: Ganglion (synovial) cystCyst of clear mucinous fluid, usually on the dorsum of the wrist, communicating with synovial sheaths ('Bible bump'). Leave alone, drain or excise.
Mallet fingerCannot extend the DIP joint after the extensor tendon partly tears from the base of the distal phalanx. RICE and splinting; complete avulsion fracture needs surgical pinning.
Carpal tunnel syndromeMedian nerve compression where it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum.
Ulnar (Guyon's) canalSite at the wrist where the ulnar nerve is at risk of injury; less common than compression at the elbow.

Superficial radial nerve in the snuff boxThe superficial (dorsal sensory) branch of the radial nerve, sensory to the dorsum of the hand lateral to the 4th digit, is at risk in the anatomical snuff box.

Distal radius fracture treatmentTreatment depends on age/activity and displacement: adequate analgesia, closed reduction (traction, increase deformity, correct) and casting with 3-point mold; surgical reduction if inadequate; then rehabilitation.
Scaphoid fracture complicationsTenuous retrograde blood supply: delayed diagnosis leads to nonunion, osteonecrosis and late arthrosis. Be suspicious: treat as fractured if X-ray normal.

Carpal tunnel syndromeMedian nerve compression at the wrist; night numbness/tingling in median territory, worse with flexed/extended wrist, possible APB weakness, Tinel/Phalen signs; median forearm muscles normal.
Carpal tunnel causesExtrinsic: fracture, flexor tenosynovitis, ganglia, inflammation, pregnancy, acromegaly. Intrinsic: diabetes, amyloidosis, alcohol. Very commonly idiopathic.

Carpal tunneldifferential and management: Main differential C6 radiculopathy; EMG/NCS (electromyography/nerve conduction) helps. Manage with education, overnight wrist orthosis, corticosteroid injection, carpal tunnel release.

Ulnar canal (Guyon's) syndromeUlnar nerve compression in Guyon's canal (fracture, ganglia, inflammation, handlebar neuropathy): hypoesthesia of medial 1½ digits, intrinsic hand weakness. Differential C8 radiculopathy, ulnar nerve at elbow.
Ulnar neuropathy managementEducation on hand position and pressure; relieve pressure (specialized gloves, change handlebars); Guyon's release.

boxes: Sciatic nerve injurySciatic nerve (L4-S3; tibial plus common peroneal) injury gives buttock pain or numbness radiating down the leg; causes: herniated disc, hip surgery, piriformis syndrome, intragluteal injection.
Limp after hip replacement (knowledge check)Pelvis drops on the side of the swinging leg after total hip replacement; slide asks which muscle, side and nerve (answer not on slide).
Hamstring avulsion (knowledge check)Hurdler feels a pop in posterior thigh, later extensive posterior thigh bleeding; X-ray shows an avulsion fracture.
Groin pullActive contraction and passive stretch of medial compartment muscles; bruising and pain; conservative treatment with RICE and NSAIDs.

Hip fracture presentationSudden groin/lateral thigh pain after a fall; shortened, externally rotated, abducted limb; cannot weight bear. High suspicion in elderly. AP pelvis/hip X-ray; CT if negative but suspicious.

Hip fracture work-upCheck stability (ABCs), pelvic fracture, distal pulses and sciatic nerve; ask why they fell (CBC, electrolytes, troponin, ECG, chest X-ray) and why they fractured (pathologic, osteoporosis).

Hip fracture managementSurgical fixation within 24-48 hours is standard; neck fractures: screws or arthroplasty; inter/subtrochanteric: intramedullary nail. Prevent VTE (LMWH 14-30 days), pneumonia, delirium; mobilize early.

boxes: ACL injuryNon-contact cutting/pivoting on deceleration; female 4.5:1. 'Pop', immediate hemarthrosis, giving way. Lachman, anterior drawer, pivot shift; MRI if unclear; reconstruction; return to play 9-12 months.

PCL injuryDirect blow to anterior tibia with knee flexed (dashboard) or hyperextension; poorly defined pain, minimal swelling. Posterior drawer, sag sign, reverse Lachman; physiotherapy usually sufficient.
MCL and LCL injuriesMCL: very common, valgus collision, minimal swelling, early range of motion and bracing. LCL: uncommon alone, high-energy varus, associated with PCL injury.

Meniscal injuriesRotation with foot planted; joint line pain, delayed swelling, locking/catching. McMurray and Thessaly tests; MRI if failing conservative care. Repair vs resection depends on zone and age.
Unhappy triadForced valgus tears the MCL, then a bucket-handle tear of the attached medial meniscus, then abduction, external rotation and slight flexion tear the ACL.
Screw-home mechanismFemur rotates medially on tibia in the last 15-20 degrees of extension, tightening the ligaments; popliteus laterally rotates the femur 5 degrees to unlock.

Patellofemoral pain syndromeAnterior knee ache after loading, prolonged sitting, stairs; no swelling. Females, adolescents, increased Q-angle. Clinical diagnosis; physiotherapy balancing vastus lateralis and vastus medialis.
Knee bursitisPrepatellar, infrapatellar, suprapatellar bursae; friction irritation; mild swelling and tenderness over the bursa. PRICE, NSAIDs. Don't confuse with septic bursitis.

Popliteal (Baker's) cystSynovial extension through posterior capsule defects into the popliteal fossa. Ultrasound confirms. Differential: popliteal artery aneurysm, DVT (deep vein thrombosis), tumour, meniscal cyst. Conservative 6 weeks.
IT band friction syndromeFriction between ITB and lateral epicondyle below 30 degrees of flexion; running, especially downhill. Aching lateral knee. PRICE, stretch ITB.
Traumatic knee swelling timingSwelling under 6 hours: ACL tear, fracture, patellar dislocation, large chondral injury. Over 6 hours: OA flare, meniscal, PCL, high-grade MCL.

Knee injectionsCorticosteroid: rapid, cheap, short-acting. Hyaluronic acid: over 26 weeks relief, expensive. PRP: no clinically significant benefit on Cochrane review. Stem cells: unproven, regulated as drugs.

Four compartments of the legAnterior (dorsiflexion, deep fibular nerve), lateral (eversion, superficial fibular nerve), superficial posterior (plantarflexion, tibial nerve), deep posterior (tibial nerve, under flexor retinaculum).

Venous return and varicose veinsValves, arteriovenous and musculovenous pumps return blood. Dilated great saphenous vein with incompetent valves gives varicose veins; laser treatment scars the vein closed.

Achilles tendinopathy and ruptureRunners after training increase; posterior heel pain, worse with passive dorsiflexion. Eccentric strengthening. Rupture in active 30-40s; surgery vs casting, surgery risks sural nerve injury.
Plantar fasciitisChronic insertional inflammation; anteromedial calcaneal pain on first morning steps, 40-60 years, F>M; tight Achilles. Heel pad, arch support, stretching, night splints.
Lateral ankle sprainUp to 85% of sprains; inversion and plantarflexion. ATFL > CFL > PTFL. Anterior drawer test of ATFL. Early mobilization, strengthening, proprioception.
Ottawa foot and ankle rulesX-ray if malleolar/midfoot pain plus bone tenderness at either malleolus posterior edge/tip, base of 5th metatarsal, or navicular, or inability to bear weight.

Ankle fracturesUnimalleolar may be non-operative; bimalleolar (forceful eversion) and trimalleolar need surgery. Maisonneuve: forceful external rotation, interosseous ligament disruption, usually surgical.
Tibialis posterior dysfunction and pes planusTendon hypovascular distal to medial malleolus; medial ankle pain, flexible then rigid flat foot, 'too many toes' sign. Strengthening, orthoses.
Bunions (hallux valgus)Footwear and metatarsus varus; medial first MTP (metatarsophalangeal) pain; poor toe-off. Wider toe box; surgical realignment.
Morton's neuromaPerineural fibrosis of common digital nerve, usually between 3rd and 4th metatarsals; burning dysesthesia, worse in narrow high heels; squeeze test.
Diabetic footMicrovascular disease and neuropathy cause insensate foot, intrinsic atrophy, Charcot joint, ulcers (15% of diabetics). Monofilament test, proper footwear, daily foot checks.
Arterial pulses of the footAbsent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests arterial disease; five P's of occlusion. Posterior tibial pulse between medial malleolus and calcaneal tendon, compare sides.
